title: The universe is making fewer stars, and the hydrogen is still there
freshness: Published in Nature Astronomy on 1 September 2026.
excerpt: FAST and DESI, used together on about 2.5 million galaxies across nearly one-third of the sky, find that the cosmic star formation rate was 2.46 times higher 4.5 billion years ago than it is today. The Chinese Academy of Sciences summary rounds that factor to about 2.5. Neutral atomic hydrogen, measured with the 21-centimetre line, was only about 1.4 times denser then. The mismatch points away from an empty fuel tank.
whyItMatters: A fading star formation rate is often blamed on galaxies running out of gas. Here the atomic hydrogen thinned only modestly while star formation fell by a much larger factor. The useful next question is how galaxies turn atomic hydrogen into the molecular gas that actually forms stars, and why that step grew less efficient as gas from the cosmic web thinned.

exploreFurther.label: Nature Astronomy: Weak evolution of cosmic atomic hydrogen over the past 4.5 billion years

whatToExploreNext: Follow the path from atomic hydrogen in the cosmic web to molecular clouds, and ask which step stalls when star formation slows.
body:
## The factory slowed. The tank barely did.

Stars do not form from the hydrogen you can count most easily. They form from molecular hydrogen, two atoms bound together, inside cold dense clouds. The larger stockpile is neutral atomic hydrogen, a single atom with its electron still attached. Astronomers abbreviate that gas as HI. It is the intermediate reservoir: gathered into a galaxy, not yet a molecule, not yet a star.

A Nature Astronomy paper published on 1 September 2026 puts two clocks side by side over the past 4.5 billion years. Star formation was faster in the past. The paper's figure is a factor of 2.46. The cosmic star formation rate 4.5 billion years ago was about 2.46 times the rate today. The Chinese Academy of Sciences summary, distributed through EurekAlert, rounds that same change to about 2.5 times. The precise factor belongs to the paper. The round number belongs to the CAS account. Name the source, and the two wordings describe the same drop.

Neutral atomic hydrogen refused to follow the same drop. Its density 4.5 billion years ago was only about 1.4 times the density today. That pairing is the measurement. A star factory slowed by more than a factor of two. The atomic tank thinned by a much smaller factor.

## A faint line, stacked across a third of the sky

HI announces itself with radio light at a wavelength of 21 centimetres. The line is faint. A single distant galaxy rarely delivers a clean detection on its own. The team used spectral stacking. Take many galaxies whose distances are already known, shift each spectrum so the expected line lands in the same channel, and add them. Noise averages down. The mean HI signal comes up.

The distances come from DESI, the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument, which supplies the redshifts. The radio spectra come from FAST, China's large radio telescope. Together the datasets cover about 2.5 million galaxies and nearly one-third of the sky. The institutions leading the work are the National Astronomical Observatories of China, the Shanghai Astronomical Observatory, and Shanghai Jiao Tong University, with DESI collaborators.

Stacking is built for an average. It will not name the cloud in a particular spiral that failed to collapse. It will say that, across a huge slice of the recent universe, newborn stars and atomic gas parted company. The journal article, DOI 10.1038/s41550-026-02965-9, is the place to read both curves. The CAS summary is the institutional account of the same result.

## The empty-tank story does not fit the gas

For years a simple story traveled with the fading of cosmic starlight. Galaxies used up their fuel. If depletion were the whole tale, the HI reservoir should have fallen about as hard as the star formation rate. It did not. The gas is still there, in the limited sense that its density changed far less than the rate at which stars were being made.

The team's interpretation is a different sentence, and it should stay labeled as an interpretation. This is not a simple fuel crisis. Conversion of HI into molecular hydrogen became less efficient. Two changes sit under that reading. Supply from the cosmic web weakened, so less fresh gas streamed in from outside galaxies. Gas density fell, and lower density makes it harder for atoms to meet, stick, and become H2.

Think of a kitchen. The pantry is only a little emptier than it was. The meals coming out have fallen by the paper's factor of 2.46. The slow step is the cooking. The shelf still holds flour. Molecular hydrogen is the ingredient that actually collapses into stars. HI is that flour, still sitting on the counter.

## What these factors will not decide

Nothing in the stack measures one disk's turbulence, one black hole's push, or one bar stirring a single galaxy. Hot halos, stellar feedback, and messy orbits can all change how fast atomic gas becomes molecular. Those are local ways the same bottleneck can appear. This survey averages them into one cosmic trend.

Keep the numbers glued to the right curves. The factor 2.46, or about 2.5 in the CAS wording, describes star formation. About 1.4 describes the HI density. Swap them and you invent either a crisis or a surplus the data do not show.

A last distinction is small enough to carry around. The 21-centimetre line counts atomic hydrogen. Star formation counts what happened after that gas became molecular and collapsed. A universe with a large HI reservoir can still look quiet in starlight, if the step between the atom and the molecule has grown clumsy. The paper measures the two trends. The efficiency story is how the team reads the gap between them.
